body: This appears to be a request for a performance improvement by a specific browser, in this case Chromium. Please file such bugs against the browser's issue tracker, in this case https://crbug.new/.

Hi @domenic, I can see why you think that at a first glance. I should have made myself more clear: I believe that imposing CSS string serialisation to change the color of shapes is a flaw in the API design that is slowing down all browser rendering engines. Firefox is the other browser currently installed on my laptop. I can observe similar overhead there. Here's a screenshot from Firefox's dev-tools performance tab's flame graph: which seems to spend most of its time is doing costly CSS parsing and color computations (a lot of the other internal calls have similar names) --- I don't see a technical reason why changing a shape's color should incur significant overhead, but I'm not a graphics person, so please correct me if I'm wrong. As far as I know it just means that you're putting different RGB values in a buffer that you're sending to the GPU or setting different RGB-values directly in a framebuffer, depending on the rendering backend. With a method like `setStrokeStrokeRGB(, , )` I'd think that each channel value would be passed as a small integer representation directly in CPU registers, after the JS-engine has JIT-compiled the calling code, meaning that the the RGB values can be directly written to the GPU buffer or framebuffer. Maybe it'd be a good idea to mask or clamp each channel value to ensure they're in the 0-255 range and/or jump to some code that throws an error if not, but that's all the overhead I'd expect. Maybe past work has been done to introduce fast paths that avoid the CSS-string serialisation overhead in browsers, but I haven't been able to hit them in the numerous implementation variations that I tested, so I'm assuming that many other users of the API will run into similar issues. Even with a fast path, this would add significant complexity to browser implementation that could be avoided with different/extended API. To maintain consistency with CSS, I can see why it's attractive to set the color using a string, but in cases where it starts becoming a problem there should be an alternative that "just works" as expected. Changing the color seems like a pretty elementary part of any graphics API: I think it's a good idea to have a simple way to do this that people can just use and not spend any more time thinking about. Hope that's clear. Thanks for your time and consideration :)

I don't think string-parsing is a significant overhead here, given that it's used for many high-performance parts of the web platform. But I think the browser teams are better equipped to answer that decisively if you get in touch with them via their bug trackers.

From what I can see from the dev-tools it does seem to be causing significant overhead, as shown -- happily make your own measurements, if I'm wrong. Numbers are generally faster than strings in all data structures and algorithms, no?

To be honest, it's coming across a bit like your just trying to defer me to someone else to avoid having to deal with this issue. Sorry if that's a mischaracterization of your intent. In my view this is a real flaw with the API design, not the implementations.

I'm not willing to spend too much time on this, so having to jump through bureaucratic hoops will achieve the goal of killing this issue if that's your intent

My current plan to remedy the overhead in my implementation is to switch to WebGL and probably draw a bunch of circles using a vertex shader. This would give a ball-park of how fast things could be. I'll keep you posted when I get that done, with some more screenshots. Maybe it's best to continue the conversation then? Form there I willing to do some benchmarking to obtain more accurate numbers or do further investigation of rendering engine internals if you think that this issue has a chance of enacting change; otherwise, I'd rather not waste time

I think Domenic's point is that implementers would know better if a specs change is really needed or if they can find a way to improve it with the current API. So at this stage, it's best that this goes through an implementer before proposing a new API shape that might not match the reality of implementations.  

Of note, https://issues.chromium.org/issues/40811924 already touched that subject. From there it was acknowledged that indeed switching styles has some overhead. It was also expected that the incoming `CSSColorValue` would indeed offer a fast path to change the color styles without requiring parsing. I didn't test myself this assertion, so I can't say if that's the case or not in Chrome's implementation.

Finally, even if `stroke()` does take very little time on the CPU, it will actually probably be the biggest bottleneck on the GPU. A common trick is to build bigger paths of a single color rather than many small paths.

Hi @Kaiido, thanks for the clarification and apologies to @domenic for the misinterpretation. I'll take a look at the chromium issue to see if there's anything of use there that I can add. Chunking draw calls into batches of same-colored shapes makes sense but I'd think that the main speedup comes from saved bandwidth sending less colors to the GPU and GPU memory needed to store colors... Still unsure how significant that'd be for performance. But unfortunately we're getting into the territory where I'm dangerously under-informed
